transcript: I think the Senate Democrats have demonstrated that with even a razor thin majority, they have the capacity to drive serious legislative content forward. What they're not going to have is the option of reconciliation. I think as the Republican selection of a speaker settles down and as committees are chosen, you're going to see the House, which is going to become an effective barrier in a lot of respect to major legislative initiatives from the left. You're also going to see a potential for a rethinking of the house as a legislative body. For too long, basically a strong speaker system has existed that has allowed Nancy Pelosi and others to function effectively as a lot of crowds. That is not the way the political culture of the house has drifted in recent years. And I think what you're likely to see is a couple of things. One, I think there will be legislative activity this year, but it's not going to be big ideological initiatives. What it is going to be is technical improvements, corrections, and small ball legislation done within committees with a certain amount of bipartisan participation, and then rolled out on the floor of the House. There are a couple of obvious places to look for this to happen, with GT Thompson of Pennsylvania as the new chairman of the Agriculture Committee, GT is going to be doing a farm bill, and although there's been some skepticism, I think there is a bipartisan base there to put together a working farm bill that can pass in this Congress. I think you're also going to see, you're probably not going to see a budget pass, both houses, although you have Mr. Boyle, and Mr. Spock are both in critical positions in the house on this. What you're likely to see is two very different budget authorities developed for each house and then kind of wave through. So in terms of a response to the budget and to appropriations, you're going to see very difficult different results in the Senate and in the house. You're also going to see I think some very interesting opportunities to sharpen legislation and develop it in some areas that have been neglected. For example, I think you're going to see Mr. Kelly of Northwestern, Pennsylvania, cheering a subcommittee of the Ways and Means Committee with the opportunity to seriously develop new tax legislation and work through the details. What we've had for the past couple of sessions has been severe ideological friction and partisan differences. What I think you have the potential to see now is at the committee level, below the level of leadership, the opportunity for some bipartisan interaction, and with Pennsylvanians playing a critical role in making that happen. So I'm telling people that I'm working with to look for strategies to move issues at the committee level and be prepared to develop champions on both sides of the aisle because bipartisanship is going to be necessary to move legislation forward.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: I think there are, but it remains to be seen whether the administration is going to aggressively pursue them. We know that the Biden administration campaign as being prepared to do something fundamentally different on trade, and they were critics of the overhaul of trade policy that came through the Trump administration. And frankly, The chamber also pointed out some of the flaws in trade policy over the past few years. But in the aftermath of the Trump administration now that we have passed the USMCA, there are some core issues that many people expected would be addressed that haven't moved forward. For example, steel tariffs is a good example. Trade sanctions were expected to be modified much more than they have been. So where does all of this leave us? I think the administration is going to have an opportunity in the next two years to decide when and how and in what form they pursue trade promotion authority. If they're prepared to do that, they have a number of potential trading partners where they could put together free trade agreements that would be appealing across the political spectrum. For example, we're very interested in my firm in the free trade agreement with Kenya that has been talked about for a number of years. I think there is still a potential for a major trade initiative with the EU, although that has become more and more difficult. This administration I think is less closely aligned than the last one. with Great Britain on the possibility of a free trade agreement there. But I think in general, there's a recognition that we need a stronger, more consistent trade policy. And there are going to be opportunities. The big issue that I think is going to be unifying across political lines is going to be the whole question of China, not only the 301 tariffs but also the issues of forced labor and violations of intellectual property and more recently China's clear efforts to circumvent countervailing duties. By passing the chips bill in the last Congress on a bipartisan basis, I think Congress set the stage for a much stronger China policy for a reshoring of certain kinds of manufacturing and for a better protection of our technology. I think the new Indo-Pacific economic framework has the potential to produce some very fertile changes in trade policy that I think could be very, very significant for the long haul. So trade promotion authority, which I think the administration has to look into themselves and ask for, I think that some of the traditional issues like GFP and a miscellaneous tariff bill are always out there. But those issues, sanctions, there is a strong trade team in this administration between Geno Ramondo, the Commerce Secretary, and Catherine by the USTR. I think if they're given the green light, they have the potential to move forward and make real progress in this space. But we're going to continue to have a certain amount of friction with our European allies because of perceptions on both sides of protectionism. And particularly, I want to be sure I make this point. When we saw the environmental initiatives passed by Congress last time, largely incentives for new green technologies, they had significant domestic preferences. built into them as tax provisions. Those have been partially waived vis-a-vis Europe, but not completely. And I think those things are going to continue to be a potential irritant, particularly because of the priority that the administration places not only on trade, but also on climate change initiatives. I don't know how Alex feels about this, but I think trade is one of the areas where there could be a certain level of bipartisanship and potentially some very new policies.
